title: Developing data awareness in data science education for empowerment in a data-driven world
text_snippet: Developing data awareness in data science education for empowerment in a data-driven world Abstract In a data-driven world, where digital technologies and infrastructures continuously collect, process, and use data about their users, thereby making users subjects of data practices embedded in digital applications such as social media platforms, search engines, and streaming services, preparing students to navigate and critically engage with such environments has become an important goal for education. Research indicates that many students lack an understanding of these data practices, feel powerless in relation to them, and therefore adopt passive roles. Educational approaches are thus needed that empower students. This raises a conceptual challenge for statistical and computing education: How can educational approaches support students and enable them to engage with these data practices in informed and reflective ways? We compare data awareness from computing education with critical statistical literacy using the ReVEAL model. Selected for their complementary nature, these approaches inform a proposed integration connecting understanding continuous data practices, evaluating statistical evidence, and reflecting on power and possibilities for individual and collective ac

title: Conceptualizing Data Literacy for Citizenship
text_snippet: Conceptualizing Data Literacy for Citizenship Abstract This survey paper opens a Special Issue of ZDM – Mathematics Education on “Enhancing data literacy for citizenship: Innovative approaches in data science and statistics education.” In this paper we aim to conceptualize ‘data literacy for citizenship’ (DataLitCit), going beyond prior conceptualizations of statistical and data literacies. We propose a working definition of DataLitCit that integrates notions of citizenship with the landscape of statistical and data literacies, and elaborate on four key areas that we consider particularly relevant for developing DataLitCit, including: criticality, data argumentation and evidentiary practices, models and modeling, and creating a bridge to AI literacy. We end with a discussion of the key contributions of the paper, and implications for education and future research directions.

title: Addressing the problem of “problem solving”
text_snippet: Addressing the problem of “problem solving” Abstract “Problem Solving” has been taken to mean many different things. On the one hand, the origin of problem solving in school mathematics must be credited to George Pólya. Pólya’s conception of problem solving encompassed the full breadth of mathematical sense-making, which includes: seeking, finding, and representing patterns; making conjectures and reasoning productively about them; and using a range of techniques to make progress on, and solve, problems that represent non-trivial challenges for the individuals working on them. On the other hand, “problem solving” in school curricula has at times been taken to mean implementing rote procedures to obtain the answers to simple exercises that students have been taught to solve. This essay traces the many meanings of “problem solving” from the mid-20th century to the present and offers the author’s opinion regarding potentially productive curricular and research directions regarding mathematical sense-making, in the spirit of Pólya’s intentions.

title: A model of evidentiary practices based on secondary students’ evaluation of media claims using complex data
text_snippet: A model of evidentiary practices based on secondary students’ evaluation of media claims using complex data Abstract The practices required to evaluate claims in the media based on mathematics and statistics are essential for informed citizenship. How the mathematical and statistical capabilities developed in school translate into these practices, however, is not well understood. In this article, we present a typology and related model of evidentiary practices based on Australian Year 10 students’ evaluation of media claims about global poverty using complex datasets. The typology and model were developed via a synthesis of research literature and an iterative process of data collection and analysis. Data drew on transcriptions of computer screen casting of student activity when working on a task based on two media items with conflicting claims. Students were provided with access to four publicly accessible datasets from credible sources. Analysis identified how students drew upon evidentiary practices when evaluating media items.

title: Relationality in civic data investigation: three cases of relational dilemmas
text_snippet: Relationality in civic data investigation: three cases of relational dilemmas Abstract Drawing on the construct of relationality — reciprocal relations of answerability between actors – we bring a lens to data literacy for citizenship that centers around the question of how relationality is embedded throughout the data investigation process. To better understand the processes for learning to engage with data investigations necessitated by the evolving complexities of society, our research examines relational dilemmas —conflicts or tensions experienced during three data investigation projects that focused on civic issues. Specifically, our analysis asks, (1) What was the nature of the relational dilemmas that arose? and (2) How did orientations to relationality guide navigation of the relational dilemma in each case? We explore these questions and examine the importance of relationality across three projects to identify possibilities, tensions, and lessons learned. We employ an exploratory multi-case study to better understand the phenomena of relational dilemmas inherent within data investigations for citizenship. Findings contribute to furthering the understanding in our field of the phenomenon of relational dilemmas in civic data investigations and to rese

title: Investigating the role of simulation-based inference in fostering critical citizenship
text_snippet: Investigating the role of simulation-based inference in fostering critical citizenship Abstract As societies become increasingly data-rich, statistics education has an important role to play in preparing students to critically examine evidence related to complex social issues. This study reports on how a statistical investigation using traffic stop data can be designed to support students in developing critical citizenship. The design drew on the statistical investigation process, Freire’s Culture Circles, and QuantCrit, to create learning experiences that integrated statistical reasoning with sociopolitical context. Fifty college students in the United States participated in seven implementations of the module, which was refined over time. Analysis of the students’ final written reports pointed to simulation-based inference as a key feature in students acknowledging institutional racism as a reason for the observed racial disparities. However, the students also needed explicit contextual support to acknowledge institutional racism. We conclude by proposing transferable principles from our design that can inform future work.

title: Exploring student discourses on AI-informed citizenship in mathematics education
text_snippet: Exploring student discourses on AI-informed citizenship in mathematics education Abstract This article explores how upper secondary students position themselves when mathematics education engages in critical, ethical and societal perspectives on AI and data driven practices based on machine learning and online digital traces. Mathematics lessons were designed and conducted to cover how data on citizens are used in machine learning to build mathematical prediction models. Such models are becoming increasingly capable due to the growing availability of digital data and advances in AI technology, and they play an increasingly prominent role in society. The lessons were designed to elucidate connections between properties in the data and properties in models, and what societal ramifications those models can have. A Foucault-inspired discourse analysis was conducted on classroom video recordings and post-intervention interviews. The analysis focused on mathematics, data, and ethics in relation to data-driven practices in society. Four discourses were construed in the discourse analysis: Choices in AI modeling have a societal impact, Accuracy is the solution to ethical issues, Data practices in society are unchallengeable, and Mathematics and ethics are incommensurab

title: Describing preservice secondary mathematics teachers’ critical statistical literacy habits of mind enactment
text_snippet: Describing preservice secondary mathematics teachers’ critical statistical literacy habits of mind enactment Abstract Globally, school standards documents increasingly emphasize statistical literacy from the consumer orientation (making sense of real-world data representations). This orientation requires the adoption of a Critical lens (e.g., focus on power and equity) because how statistics are used (e.g., decision making) cannot be separated from the fact that social issues operate within systems of marginalization, privilege, and power. This study aims to explore how preservice secondary mathematics teachers enact critical statistical literacy habits of mind (CSLHM) when presented with data representations from the media. Findings reveal that preservice mathematics teachers typically emergently enact CSLHM, and some robustly. There is no evidence from this study, that the preservice secondary mathematics teachers enact CSLHM habitually (no PSTs enacted all six CSLHM across each post), but are capable of enacting them independently. The findings suggest that preservice secondary mathematics teachers need support and opportunities to robustly enact CSLHM. title: Comparing different pathways to primary mathematics teaching using teacher competence measurement of the TEDS research program
text_snippet: Comparing different pathways to primary mathematics teaching using teacher competence measurement of the TEDS research program Abstract Teacher shortages are a major challenge worldwide, especially in mathematics. In response, many countries have implemented measures to recruit graduates from fields other than mathematics teaching for alternative pathways into the teaching profession, offering an alternative fast-track qualification pathway. Such a pathway was implemented in North Rhine-Westphalia (Germany) within the second phase of teacher education—the so-called induction phase—combined with a six-month preparatory phase. As it remains unclear to what extent the teaching proficiency of these out-of-field teachers is comparable to that of teachers from traditional teacher education pathways, a large-scale study was conducted covering alternatively and traditionally educated primary preservice teachers (PSTs) with a focus on mathematics. A sample of 444 alternatively (A-PSTs) and traditionally trained preservice teachers (T-PSTs) was assessed using standardized test instruments developed within the research program stemming from the Teacher Education and Development Study in Mathematics (TEDS-M). title: Expanding mathematical teaching practices of out-of-field teachers of secondary mathematics
text_snippet: Expanding mathematical teaching practices of out-of-field teachers of secondary mathematics Abstract An insufficient number of qualified secondary mathematics teachers available to teach mathematics has existed for decades. Pre 2020, addressing the phenomenon of out-of-field mathematics teaching was an Australia education policy priority and government investments in professional learning initiatives were made. The purpose of the research reported here is to examine approaches used to support such teachers through a post-graduate course for Years 7-10 teachers teaching mathematics out-of-field. Design-based research was applied to design novel learning opportunities focused on extending teachers’ curricular knowledge, mathematical content knowledge, mathematical pedagogical content knowledge, and readiness to use mathematical digital technologies (mathematical digital technological knowledge). We examine communication media posts during the course and students’ reflections on the course in post course interviews to illustrate the impact of the approach. title: Conceptualizing critical data education
text_snippet: Conceptualizing critical data education Abstract There are many conceptual papers on what critical literacy/pedagogy might entail in statistics education, data science education, and data literacy. However, they exist disjointly in the literature creating problems with coherence and translating findings–leading to duplicate work and missed opportunities. In this paper, we addressed this issue by synthesizing the literature on critical perspectives in statistics education, data science education, and data literacy to create a conception of a critical data education for critical citizenship. Our aim is to establish a shared conceptual foundation to guide and encourage future educational research that could be used across disciplinary boundaries in K-12 education and teacher education and inform pedagogical work.

title: Insights into professional development for junior secondary mathematics teachers viewed as out-of-field – a South African case
text_snippet: Insights into professional development for junior secondary mathematics teachers viewed as out-of-field – a South African case Abstract Out-of-field (OOF) mathematics teaching is complex and context-dependent, particularly where formal qualifications do not adequately reflect teachers’ preparedness. Drawing on a longitudinal professional development (PD) programme for junior secondary mathematics teachers in South African schools serving low-income communities, this paper broadens the conceptualisation of OOF teaching and distils principles for context-relevant PD. We describe a sustained mathematics-for-teaching course that prioritised mathematical knowledge while explicitly mediating mathematics teaching practices. Teacher assessments and a quasi-experimental learner study showed significant gains in teachers’ mathematical knowledge and modest but significant gains in learner attainment, with indications that learner impact may be delayed. These findings support extending OOF beyond formal qualification criteria to include teachers who self-identify as underprepared. We propose principles for sustained, context-conscious PD that works “with the grain” of existing practices, bringing evidence from the Global South to a predominantly Global North literature.

title: Educative features of formative assessment curriculum materials: the cases of MAP and MesiMatica
text_snippet: Educative features of formative assessment curriculum materials: the cases of MAP and MesiMatica Abstract Formative assessment (FA) is recognized as a core instructional practice in mathematics education, yet it is not widely embedded in mathematics instruction. Little is known about how curriculum materials support teachers’ learning to enact FA. Drawing on the framework of educative curriculum materials, this study offers a comparative analysis of a purposively selected sample of units from two well-established FA-oriented initiatives in secondary mathematics: the Mathematics Assessment Project and MesiMatica. The analysis examines how each set of materials embeds educative support through three dimensions: the rationale articulated to teachers, the knowledge made available, and the guidance provided for implementation. Attention is given to how guidance is configured in terms of specificity and flexibility across the phases of eliciting, interpreting, and responding to evidence of student learning. Findings show that while both initiatives combine high specificity with flexibility, they distribute these features differently across the FA process, illustrating alternative design logics for supporting teachers’ learning to enact FA.

title: The interplay of task difficulty, precision and feedback in students’ help-seeking behaviour in online maths environments
text_snippet: The interplay of task difficulty, precision and feedback in students’ help-seeking behaviour in online maths environments Abstract Online mathematics environments often provide feedback to support students’ mathematical learning. The extent to which students make use of feedback, so-called ‘help-seeking’, depends on numerous instructional variables, including the type of online platform, task difficulty and students’ precision. However, most student behaviour in such platforms occurs outside the view of the teacher, and engagements with such environments are not independent events: the order in which tasks are completed matters. This paper reports on two education phases where we explore the interplay of task difficulty, precision and feedback in two online mathematics environments. We use log file data from both platforms and analyse them with multivariate regression and sequence analysis. Study 1 uses student data from English students in grades 3 to 5 ( $N=839$ N = 839 ), totalling 490,426 records. Study 2 uses data from undergraduate mathematics students ( $N=232$ N = 232 ), totalling 138,632 records. The results show that task difficulty, precision and feedback interact, with help-seeking not necessarily relating to higher task difficulty or precision. title: Analyzing high school students’ critical ethical decision-making in data science
text_snippet: Analyzing high school students’ critical ethical decision-making in data science Abstract As society increasingly relies on Big Data Analytics, there is an urgent need for critical ethical decision-makers who can navigate the risks of data-driven harm. At present, educators lack analytic tools to understand how students make these complex ethical choices. This paper introduces the Ethical Decision Making in Data Science Framework, an analytic tool built on critical mathematics, relational and normative ethics, to characterize student reasoning and agency. We demonstrate the framework by analyzing high school students’ reasoning from task-based interviews following a Critical Ethical Data Science course. Our findings highlight the specific knowledge bases and reasoning practices necessary to cultivate critical ethical data science practitioners.

title: Same variable, different values? A multilevel Latent Transition Analysis of students’ thinking about values of variables
text_snippet: Same variable, different values? A multilevel Latent Transition Analysis of students’ thinking about values of variables Abstract Understanding the values that variables can take is a central challenge in students’ early encounters with algebra. While previous research has documented a range of numerical preconceptions related to variable values, much less is known about how they co-occur and develop. This study examines German Year 7/8 students’ (mis)understandings of variable values before and after four weeks of regular algebra teaching. Data were collected from 2205 students who completed the SMART ‘Values for Letters’ test. The test targets well-documented numerical preconceptions, including difficulties with substituting given values, alphabet-based value assumptions, treating multiple occurrences of the same letter as referring to independent values, and assuming that different letters must represent different numbers. To capture qualitative differences in students’ response patterns and their development over time, we applied multilevel Latent Transition Analysis (LTA), accounting for students nested within teachers. title: Lesson study and virtual exchange as a context to involve mathematics preservice teachers with inclusive education
text_snippet: Lesson study and virtual exchange as a context to involve mathematics preservice teachers with inclusive education Abstract Current curriculum documents underline the need to develop inclusive education. Participating in lesson study is an opportunity for mathematics preservice teachers to engage with ideas in this field. In addition, exchange activities between preservice teachers from different countries is a way to strengthen a positive disposition towards the profession, while contributing to the development and consolidation of professional knowledge. Thus, our aim is to know how preservice teachers from two countries engage with inclusive education ideas in the context of lesson study supported in a virtual environment. This research is qualitative and is based on a collaborative exchange in the first semester of 2025 between preservice teachers of three different universities, two in Brazil and one in Portugal. The exchange activities were held online based on the Zoom platform and offline using Google Drive and Google Docs. The preservice teachers were in the final stages of their initial teacher education preparation. title: Artificial intelligence in mathematics education: a two-dimensional conceptual framework and meta-review
text_snippet: Artificial intelligence in mathematics education: a two-dimensional conceptual framework and meta-review Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming mathematics education just as it is reshaping many other domains of modern life, creating new opportunities that fundamentally change the way students and teachers work. AI has become an increasingly prominent topic in mathematics education, generating a growing body of systematic reviews. However, the review-level literature remains fragmented across different AI paradigms, system types, and methodological approaches. This meta-review synthesizes existing systematic reviews on AI in mathematics education and provides a conceptually oriented interpretation of how AI is shaping mathematics education. We specifically identify and classify the types of AI present in mathematics education as well as the educational functions it fulfills. To organize the synthesis, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes between a technological dimension of AI, referring to major AI paradigms and system types, and a functional dimension, referring to the educational roles AI can serve in mathematics education. title: Students’ mathematical feedback processes using a digital curriculum resource: a qualitative perspective
text_snippet: Students’ mathematical feedback processes using a digital curriculum resource: a qualitative perspective Abstract This qualitative case study investigates how automated feedback from a widely accessible digital curriculum resource influences students’ mathematics learning. Drawing on a dialogic feedback framework, the study analyzes students’ feedback processes in an ecologically valid learning context. Grounded in a sociocultural perspective, the framework integrates Carless’ dialogic conceptualization of feedback, Shute’s feedback typology, and Vergnaud’s scheme theory. Eight eighth-graders from a German secondary school worked individually on percentage problems at home, video-recorded via online conferencing. Data included screen recordings and think-aloud protocols, which were analyzed using qualitative text analysis. Results reveal large individual differences in feedback processes—students vary in when and how they access feedback messages and how they make sense of them. Successfully solving a task after feedback does not always indicate understanding; in some cases, feedback aided procedural completion without conceptual insight. title: Explaining mathematics teachers’ class test design and its relation to feedback: an explorative study in Germany and Italy
text_snippet: Explaining mathematics teachers’ class test design and its relation to feedback: an explorative study in Germany and Italy Abstract Class tests are a crucial part of written classroom assessment in mathematics. They are designed by teachers, can address summative and formative purposes and can be expected to provide feedback that informs teaching and supports student learning. This potential seems often underused, and little is known about criteria guiding teachers’ design decisions. This binational interview study conducted with secondary school teachers from Germany and Italy investigates how they design class tests, which criteria they apply, and how feedback is considered across different phases of assessment. To situate interview analyses within teachers’ professional context, we present a conceptual framework that conceives class tests as part of an assessment cycle linking operationalisation, measurement, validation, and feedback. With reference to this framework, results from qualitative interview analyses indicate that task selection is mainly guided by implicit and routinised criteria, is only loosely connected to formal competence frameworks or cognitive-demand considerations and that institutional, collegial, and socio-cultural influences strongly shape teachers’ decisions in both countries

title: Running on empty: motivation, commitment, goodwill and the needs of secondary school out-of-field mathematics teachers
text_snippet: Running on empty: motivation, commitment, goodwill and the needs of secondary school out-of-field mathematics teachers Abstract Teacher shortages in secondary schools remain a significant issue in Australia and internationally, with ongoing shortages of qualified mathematics teachers contributing to out-of-field (OOF) teaching. This qualitative study, guided by situated expectancy-value theory, examined school staff decision-making by 18 school leaders and 8 mathematics Head Teachers (HTs), and experiences of 17 OOF and 14 infield mathematics teachers. Data from 57 interviews across eight diverse government secondary schools in New South Wales, Australia, were interpretatively analysed. Findings showed leaders prefer to assign ‘good’ teachers to teach junior secondary mathematics OOF, who can manage classes, build positive relationships with students, and are willing. HTs prioritised classroom management, strong relationships with students, and sufficient mathematical skills. OOF teachers generally approached the role with goodwill but required additional preparation time and help to engage all students. Infield teachers supported them through resources, explanations, mentoring, and confidence building. Recommendations for future research and policy are offered.

title: Non-specialist primary school mathematics teachers’ beliefs
text_snippet: Non-specialist primary school mathematics teachers’ beliefs Abstract This paper reports on a qualitative exploratory case study of four out-of-field primary school mathematics teachers in rural South Africa. The focus is on their subject knowledge and didactical expertise as aspects of their teacher identity through the lens of their beliefs about the subject. The purpose of the study was to examine whether non-specialist teachers developed a professional mathematics teacher identity through experience. The findings reveal that the participants’ lack of subject matter knowledge and didactical expertise were related to their beliefs about the nature of mathematics. The resultant weak learner performance further entrenched these teachers’ belief that mathematics is extremely difficult for teacher and learner alike. The participants demonstrated a lack of confidence, taught various mathematical concepts incorrectly, and could not explain the mathematical concepts. Their instrumentalist beliefs serve predominantly as a coping strategy, mitigating the cognitive and emotional difficulties linked to instructing a subject in which they have insufficient understanding. title: Transformative insights? An exploration of critical data literacy with undergraduate learners from Southern India
text_snippet: Transformative insights? An exploration of critical data literacy with undergraduate learners from Southern India Abstract The Civic Statistics (CS) approach promotes critical data literacy for engaged citizens; however, empirical evidence of its effectiveness remains limited. This study examines how participation in a civic statistics informed Data Science (DS) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) course relates to changes in learners’ descriptions of their technical and critical data literacy and whether these changes persist over time. The study examines a 24-hour online DS and AI course, with an extended 40 hour in-person immersion for a subset of participants. Twenty-one undergraduate engineering and computer science students from Southern India participated in the study (nine completed the extended programme). Self-report surveys were administered before the course, immediately after the online course and six months later. Thematic analysis was used to examine open-ended responses for critical data literacy dimensions (cognitions, dispositions, actions). Four themes emerged: Developing Understanding, Learner Enthusiasm, Real-world Engagement and Critical Evaluation . title: How generative AI guided-professional development supports teachers’ engagement with mathematical creativity, content knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge
text_snippet: How generative AI guided-professional development supports teachers’ engagement with mathematical creativity, content knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge Abstract This embedded case study examined how eight in-service teachers from rural and under-resourced districts engaged with mathematical creativity (MC), content knowledge (CK), and pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) during an AI-guided professional development program, and how specific AI-mediated mechanisms shaped that engagement. Teachers completed ten interactive modules in which a generative AI system served as a cognitive and instructional partner by prompting problem solving, problem posing, representational reasoning, simulated student interpretation, and reflective instructional decision-making. Data sources included teacher-AI dialogue logs, teacher-generated mathematical artifacts, and interviews, which were analyzed through iterative thematic analysis. Findings showed that teachers engaged with MC, CK, and PCK as interconnected forms of reasoning rather than as isolated domains. Three cross-case themes characterized this engagement: creative mathematical exploration, conceptual deepening of proportional reasoning, and expansion of pedagogical reasoning. title: School leader and teacher perspectives on teaching mathematics out-of-field: who, to whom, why and does it matter?
text_snippet: School leader and teacher perspectives on teaching mathematics out-of-field: who, to whom, why and does it matter? Abstract Out-of-field (OOF) teaching remains a common practice in secondary schools, particularly in mathematics where teacher shortages are prevalent. Surveys of school leaders ( $N=100$ N = 100 ) and mathematics teachers ( $N=217$ N = 217 ; of whom 97 OOF) from 48 Australian government schools explore: 1) difficulties schools leaders experience to employ qualified mathematics teachers; 2) leaders’ preferences for assigning OOF teachers to classes, comparing Principals/Deputies and Head Teachers; 3) the characteristics of OOF mathematics teachers and their reasons for teaching OOF; and 4) potential consequences of teachers teaching mathematics OOF—for themselves and the students they teach. Leaders’ preference to address shortages was recruiting retired teachers followed by sharing programs between schools. Principals/Deputies preferred requiring teachers who had availability to teach mathematics OOF, which Head Teachers wished to avoid. Both groups preferred assigning teachers skilled in mathematics, who valued mathematics more, experienced and skilled pedagogues who coped well with demands and were willing, and wished to avoid early-career teachers. title: Integrating data literacy and climate science: creating multidisciplinary, data-driven social media posts in grade 10 on human-induced climate change
text_snippet: Integrating data literacy and climate science: creating multidisciplinary, data-driven social media posts in grade 10 on human-induced climate change Abstract This study reports on a 15-hour multidisciplinary teaching unit that integrates data literacy and climate change education for grade 10 students. Grounded in social-constructivist and civic statistics principles, the unit engages learners with real datasets (global temperature, temperature and CO2 data from Vostok ice cores, and Mauna Loa CO2 data) using CODAP for visualization and piecewise trend analysis. Students create Instagram-like posts that are intended to help students integrate different disciplinary learning experiences related to climate change as a formative learning journal to communicate their data-based findings. Two classes produced 131 posts, 35 contained data-based arguments and were analyzed with qualitative content analysis against the scaffolding Statistical Communication Framework for Social Media Posts (SCFSMP). Most data-oriented posts included visualizations and described trends and patterns. Only a few to none addressed the data source, reliability of the data, or limitations of the data. title: Trajectories of out-of-field secondary mathematics teachers in New Zealand
text_snippet: Trajectories of out-of-field secondary mathematics teachers in New Zealand Abstract Persistent concerns exist internationally regarding teacher shortages and the prevalence of out-of-field teachers in secondary schools. In New Zealand, anecdotal evidence suggests growing difficulty recruiting qualified secondary mathematics teachers, yet little empirical data exist on the scale of the problem, the reliance on out-of-field teachers, or the support they receive. Drawing on communities of practice as a theoretical framework, this study reports findings from a national questionnaire of school leaders and mathematics teachers. We examined the distribution and characteristics of out-of-field teachers, the extent of recruitment difficulty, and how these varied across school contexts. We also explored the challenges they faced and the support available. Findings reveal widespread recruitment difficulties and reliance on out-of-field teachers, with patterns shaped by school size, region, and socio-economic context. Teachers’ experiences highlight the importance of collegial support in enabling progression towards fuller participation in the mathematics teaching community, although variability in support leaves some at the periphery. title: Educating data-informed citizens: statistical, political and information search efficacies and their interactions
text_snippet: Educating data-informed citizens: statistical, political and information search efficacies and their interactions Abstract Although recent initiatives in statistics education have emphasized civic and socio-political contexts, little is known about the motivational resources that support engagement with data in public life. This study investigates the relationships among statistical, political, and information-search self-efficacy and examines how these beliefs develop within an interdisciplinary civic statistics intervention. Using a pre–post-test control-group design with pre-service teachers from mathematics and civics programs, we analyzed the development of domain-specific self-efficacy beliefs and students’ appreciation of the role of science in politics. Correlation, Bayesian network, and structural equation modeling analyses revealed that statistical, political, and information-search self-efficacy are moderately related but distinct constructs, with information-search self-efficacy occupying a central position within the network. The intervention produced substantial gains in statistical self-efficacy ( $\eta ^{2} = .12$ η 2 = . 12 ) and information-search self-efficacy ( $\eta ^{2} = .11$ η 2 = . 11 ), while effects on political self-efficacy were smaller and less robust. title: LLMs as useful training tools for mathematics teachers: opportunities or hallucinations?
text_snippet: LLMs as useful training tools for mathematics teachers: opportunities or hallucinations? Abstract We explore the extent to which answers to mathematics word problems generated by AI chatbots are comparable to students’ answers, and whether interaction with them is useful for replicating classroom discourse. We use a large language model (LLM) to solve ten standard textbook exercises 100 times for each question and analyse the answers to identify tasks suitable for further interaction through teacher prompts. Based on this analysis, we derive suitable teacher interventions, in the form of follow-up prompts, and determine their impact on the LLM output. We show that LLM-generated answers can indeed resemble students’ answers and argue that these answers can be used with preservice educators as they learn to intervene productively in student learning. However, we also found that generic follow-up prompts can be more effective than specific prompts based on pedagogical content knowledge in generating a correct LLM response. Taken together, these findings suggest that LLMs may be well suited to modelling students’ mathematical solutions, but less suited to modelling how students naturally respond to instructional prompts. title: ‘I apologise for the ${T}_{{n}}$ thing’: a Swiss Cheese Model analysis of mathematics reform enactment
text_snippet: ‘I apologise for the ${T}_{{n}}$ thing’: a Swiss Cheese Model analysis of mathematics reform enactment Abstract Policymakers often assume that strengthening teacher quality through the provision of qualification upgrade programmes and reform-aligned instructional materials leads to improved teaching quality and the enactment of reform pedagogy. However, in this paper, we present the case of John, an out-of-field mathematics teacher who completed a qualification upgrade programme, to demonstrate that teaching quality can be compromised even when these reform supports are offered and utilised. Drawing on lesson observations from two timepoints, we investigate an error that emerged in John’s teaching during his participation in the programme and explore how he addressed the same content one year later, after qualifying to teach mathematics. We show that John adapted his teaching to avoid making the same error; however, we contend that these adaptations shifted his practice away from reform pedagogy and likely introduced latent vulnerabilities in students’ learning. Using the Swiss Cheese Model, we illustrate how vulnerabilities in John’s teaching across the timepoints may relate to vulnerabilities in the reform-aligned instructional materials and the design of the qualification upgrade

title: Student-designed educational resources for Lean: exploring ChatGPT and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text_snippet: Student-designed educational resources for Lean: exploring ChatGPT and Retrieval-Augmented Generation Abstract Recent technological developments are rapidly changing the teaching and learning of mathematics. Among such tools, we focus on Lean and ChatGPT, an area which remains under-researched in mathematics education. The aim of this study is to explore university students’ experience and views of creating educational resources using Lean and ChatGPT. Drawing on the framework of documentation work, we analyse the resources created by four undergraduate and one postgraduate student, who had previously used Lean and were invited to design materials to support future students learning Lean. Through an analysis of their customised ChatGPT tools using Retrieval-Augmented Generation, educational resources, and interview data, we show how students retrospectively described developing a more critical stance towards Lean and ChatGPT through their design work. Our findings highlight the diversity of documentation work with ChatGPT, shedding light on the complexities of integrating AI into mathematics education.

title: Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers’ intervention and students’ engagement in the mathematics classroom
text_snippet: Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers’ intervention and students’ engagement in the mathematics classroom Abstract Emotions play a central role in how students engage with mathematical problem-solving, yet teachers often have limited access to students’ moment-to-moment emotional experiences, particularly during independent technology-supported work. This study examines how AI-generated emotional alerts are incorporated into mathematics teachers’ real-time instructional decision-making and how teachers’ responses to these alerts participate in students’ engagement during mathematical problem-solving. Drawing on Goldin’s framework of engagement structures, which considers affect as an integral component of cognition, a qualitative case study was conducted with one teacher and eight high-achieving high school students using Dash4Emotion, an AI-generated emotional alert system. Data sources included video recordings of classroom interactions, logs of the AI-generated emotional system, and stimulus recall interviews. The findings identified five recurring patterns through which the alerts became part of the teacher’s instructional decision-making. These patterns show how the alerts directed the teacher’s attention to particular students or moments and were interpreted alongside students’ o

title: Using multimodal learning analytics to study student engagement and teacher noticing in mathematics classroom: two different human-in-the-loop workflows
text_snippet: Using multimodal learning analytics to study student engagement and teacher noticing in mathematics classroom: two different human-in-the-loop workflows Abstract “Human-in-the-loop” has been the recommended approach to incorporate AI in education research to mitigate risks associated with automation. However, currently there are no specific models or guidelines for designing or reporting on the human-in-the-loop process in education research. This theoretical paper contrasts two different ways in which human judgement and agency were incorporated in the design of two studies in mathematics education. The two studies, one on student collaborative problem solving, and one on teacher noticing and in-the-moment decision making, both used multimodal learning analytics incorporating machine learning to analyse the audiovisual data but involved human input in different ways. Through explicating the research purposes and foci of the two studies, this paper argues that how and when human input should be incorporated in the research process would depend on the research questions and the constructs of interest. By making visible decision points in the research process that incorporates human input in two concrete research examples, this paper offers researchers a reference point for designing future research that incorporates AI within mathem

title: Using webcam eye tracking and AI to determine how students proceed in basic mathematical activities: a study based on a digital adaptive learning system
text_snippet: Using webcam eye tracking and AI to determine how students proceed in basic mathematical activities: a study based on a digital adaptive learning system Abstract Many students struggle with basic mathematics, such as the understanding of numbers and arithmetic operations, even in grade 5 and higher. Previous research has shown that the difficulties are often reflected in how the students proceed when working on basic mathematics tasks. Eye tracking (ET) has proven valuable for analyzing how students proceed in such activities, for example, number line activities. However, dedicated ET equipment is typically not accessible for teachers and analyzing ET videos is too time-consuming and demanding for in-service educators. The aim of this paper is to investigate how a combination of webcam-ET and AI can help; specifically, we aim to investigate how well AI (here: Supervised Machine Learning, SML) can determine from webcam-ET data how students proceed. We developed a digital learning system called KI-ALF that uses webcam-based ET and AI to automatically identify how students proceed and collected data from 141 fifth graders, which were analyzed for this study. Our findings show that the AI is promising in determining how students proceed, yet, the quality of the identification varies between different mathematical activities, with the h

title: Out-of-field mathematics teaching and its impact on student achievement across countries: evidence from TIMSS 2023
text_snippet: Out-of-field mathematics teaching and its impact on student achievement across countries: evidence from TIMSS 2023 Abstract Although assumptions regarding out-of-field (OOF) mathematics teachers—such as their limited knowledge, motivation, or self-efficacy—are often linked to a negative influence on student achievement, empirical evidence in this regard remains inconsistent. Using TIMSS 2023 data from eighth-grade students, this study applied a Bayesian multilevel modeling framework to analyze cross-country patterns in the relationship between OOF teaching and mathematics achievement among students. The analysis included country-specific models alongside an overall international model with country fixed effects. The results revealed that, in the overall international sample, students taught by OOF teachers scored, on average, 7.7 points lower in mathematics than those taught by in-field teachers. This negative association remained consistent across all content and cognitive domains in mathematics. However, country-specific models revealed substantial variation: Finland—where 24.9% of eighth-grade students are taught OOF in mathematics—demonstrated a clear negative association, with students taught by OOF teachers scoring, on average, 14.1 points lower than those taught by in-field teachers. title: Informal approaches to predictive modeling: fostering data literacy and critical engagement through decision tree construction
text_snippet: Informal approaches to predictive modeling: fostering data literacy and critical engagement through decision tree construction Abstract This study investigates how secondary students construct and evaluate decision trees in an open exploratory task using CODAP. By analyzing students’ tree products and oral self-reports, we identified different data-based and context-based approaches to predictor selection and stopping criteria. Students engaged with key ideas of predictive modeling, including classification, model construction, accuracy, generalization, and interpretability. Informal exploration offered rich opportunities for subsequent teaching by enabling students to begin reconstructing central technical ideas and critical tensions of predictive modeling through diverse but meaningful reasoning approaches.

title: Collectives of humans-with-GenAI in university mathematical modelling: different forms of human-AI interaction in the production of mathematical knowledge
text_snippet: Collectives of humans-with-GenAI in university mathematical modelling: different forms of human-AI interaction in the production of mathematical knowledge Abstract This study applied the humans-with media perspective to examine how collectives of students-with-ChatGPT produced mathematical knowledge during a university-level mathematical modelling task. We conceptualized generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) not as an external tool, but as a participant in a mathematical (modelling) activity. The qualitative study involved 94 engineering students enrolled in a Differential Equations course and focused on three modelling stages: problem framing, mathematical development, and interpretation/validation. Data were generated from modelling reports, oral presentations, questionnaires, and semi-structured group interviews. Findings indicate that interaction with GenAI varied in the organization of agency within each collective. ChatGPT participated in problem framing and interpretive synthesis but not in mathematically rigorous development, with several groups of students restricting or rejecting its use due to limitations in symbolic manipulation and numerical accuracy. Across groups, interaction configurations ranged from mediated participation to delegative incorporation, reflecting different distributions of agency and authorship.

title: Preservice mathematics teachers’ noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping
text_snippet: Preservice mathematics teachers’ noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping Abstract Teacher noticing is a key component of teacher competence, referring to how teachers attend to, interpret, and shape classroom interactions to gain access to students’ thinking. However, less is known about how these dimensions are coordinated during ongoing interaction. This study addresses this gap by conceptualising noticing as an iterative and interactional process and examining transitions among noticing dimensions within AI-based simulations. Seventeen preservice mathematics teachers participated in a three-week intervention involving text-based interactions with AI-simulated students and mentor feedback. Data were analysed using qualitative coding and Epistemic Network Analysis. Findings show that noticing was organised through recurring transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping. Strong connections between interpreting and shaping suggest that PTs’ interpretations frequently informed subsequent inquiry moves that generated new opportunities for noticing students’ thinking. Differences across weeks further indicate the situated and context-sensitive organisation of noticing within AI-based interactions. The study contributes to demonstrating how AI-based

title: Before or after? Beyond timing of students’ interaction with generative artificial intelligence in proving mathematical statements
text_snippet: Before or after? Beyond timing of students’ interaction with generative artificial intelligence in proving mathematical statements Abstract In this study, we investigate how the sequence of interactions with generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) influences undergraduate students’ mathematical proof construction. We compared two instructional approaches: Initial genAI-Independent Proving (IIP) in which students constructed their own drafts before interacting with genAI, and Initial genAI-Dependent Proving (IDP), in which students interacted with genAI proofs before drafting their own proofs. Thirty undergraduate students participated, engaging with two related proof tasks across the instructional sessions. We analyzed how students incorporated AI-generated proofs into their work. The results show that students in both conditions incorporated AI-generated proofs to a similar extent, but differed in how they engaged with genAI during the proving process. Students in the IIP condition used genAI to revisit key components of their proofs and to revise their independently constructed proofs whereas those in the IDP condition used genAI as a reference or guide in their proof-making process. title: From surface practices to deep conceptually targeted practices for fostering students’ place value understanding: Case study on an out-of-field teacher’s professional growth
text_snippet: From surface practices to deep conceptually targeted practices for fostering students’ place value understanding: Case study on an out-of-field teacher’s professional growth Abstract For many out-of-field teachers, limitations in mathematical and pedagogical content knowledge have been identified. However, the ways in which these limitations shape their instructional practices have not been systematically explored. Furthermore, little is known about how out-of-field teachers’ practices can grow through professional development. A qualitative single-case study contributes to reducing these research gaps by comparing teaching practices. These were video-recorded before and after completing a session that provided access to pedagogical content knowledge about key concept elements for place value understanding. The comparison reveals that the teacher’s practices shift from untargeted surface practices to deep conceptually targeted practices. It disentangles how targeting concept elements supports deeper, conceptually focused instruction. Unpacking the background of substantial professional growth can contribute to emphasizing the value of topic-specific professional development opportunities.

title: AI-powered learning: exploring secondary school students’ use of ChatGPT for solving mathematical modelling problems
text_snippet: AI-powered learning: exploring secondary school students’ use of ChatGPT for solving mathematical modelling problems Abstract The rapid emergence of large language models has raised important questions about their potential to influence learning and problem-solving in real-world contexts. Mathematical modelling is particularly relevant in this regard, as it links abstract mathematical concepts to real-life situations and plays a key role in mathematics curricula. However, few studies have examined how school students use these tools in practice. This study investigates how secondary school students use ChatGPT to solve mathematical modelling problems, a core element of mathematics education. In this exploratory study, ten tenth-graders worked in pairs during a two-hour session on two modelling tasks using ChatGPT. Data sources included written work, chat logs, and semi-structured interviews. Findings show that students relied almost exclusively on zero-shot prompting; few-shot and chain-of-thought strategies were absent, and output customisation was rare. Most prompts focused on early modelling phases (simplifying, structuring, mathematising), while validation and interpretation were largely missing. title: Does subjective task value mediate the effect of digital simulation-based explorations on fraction learning? A randomized-controlled trial
text_snippet: Does subjective task value mediate the effect of digital simulation-based explorations on fraction learning? A randomized-controlled trial Abstract Fractions are challenging but essential for mathematical learning. Educational technology may support students’ acquisition of fraction concepts. This study investigates underlying cause-and-effect mechanisms, i.e., whether features, e.g., authentic simulations, have a motivating effect in learning situations—resulting in an indirect learning-promoting effect. In a randomized controlled trial with $N=292$ N = 292 sixth-grade students, we examined the effects of a digital, simulation-based exploration of fractions compared to a paper-based version on students’ subjective task value and their learning gains related to ‘part of many wholes’ concept. Results showed a significant positive effect of the digital, simulation-based exploration on a composite scale of students’ intrinsic value and attainment value. Mediation analysis further indicated that the digital simulation significantly enhanced students’ subjective task value, which in turn significantly improved posttest achievement. Consistent with the mediation hypothesis, we found a significant indirect effect. These findings underscore the importance of integrating features into digital learning environments that enhance

title: A situative perspective on motivation in mathematics education: a systematic review
text_snippet: A situative perspective on motivation in mathematics education: a systematic review Abstract Motivation has long been recognised as a key factor in students’ learning, achievement, and engagement in mathematics. In this systematic review, we examine how a situative perspective on motivation has been conceptualised, theorised, and operationalised in recent research on learning and instruction in mathematics. Specifically, we analyse the ways in which situatedness is recognised and captured across studies positioned across major motivational frameworks (i.e., expectancy-value, interest, self-determination, achievement goal, and social-cognitive theory), and the methodological approaches employed (i.e., participants, analytical methods, data sources, and measures) until the first half of 2025. Our review identifies 76 studies that focus on situatedness in the motivation for learning mathematics, the majority of which are empirical, quantitative, and employ variable-centred approaches. Across the motivational theoretical frameworks, situated expectancy-value theory is the most prevalent and survey methods dominate. title: Open science meets orange skies: K-12 educators’ engagement with computational notebooks to explore scientific events with human impacts
text_snippet: Open science meets orange skies: K-12 educators’ engagement with computational notebooks to explore scientific events with human impacts Abstract Computational notebooks are becoming a popular method to introduce mathematics, data, and scientific computing concepts to secondary students. Advocates argue computational notebooks encourage transparency and reproducibility in student work and can enable more personalized investigations of publicly available civic and scientific datasets. However, little is known about how teachers navigate these complex artifacts, let alone how they might support their students in doing so. In this paper, we investigate six pre-service and two in-service K-12 teachers’ sensemaking during a structured clinical think-aloud interview as they engaged with a computational notebook that examines disruptions in local air quality. The notebook presented a common event (annual fireworks) and an extreme event that impacted human health, during which the skies above the greater metropolitan San Francisco Bay region in California, USA turned orange due to wildfire pollution (“Orange Skies Day”, Sept 9, 2020). title: Exploring the sustaining of mathematics interest: students navigating stuckness during online small-group activity
text_snippet: Exploring the sustaining of mathematics interest: students navigating stuckness during online small-group activity Abstract Even when students’ interest is triggered by some feature of the mathematics activity with which they are working, it can be a challenge for educators to support them to sustain their interest—to begin asking their own questions about mathematics, voluntarily exploring its structure, patterns, and relations. In the present study, we examined whether student groups that persevere to navigate stuckness simply are more interested in mathematics, or if resources such as opportunities to collaborate, group-worthy problems, and an online context that required turn-taking, reflection, and discussion, supported students to sustain interest and work with stuckness. We focused on instances in which 3-5-person groups in a class of seventh-grade students (15 male, 13 female; 78.6% Hispanic) worked with stuckness during an open-ended mathematics activity in the Virtual Math Teams (VMT) environment. Data sources included continuous records of group problem-solving activity using a chat discussion and a dynamic workspace. Additional data sources included assessments of achievement, interest, level of collaboration, and use of executive functions. Group-level descriptive analyses showed t

title: Automated coding of content and pedagogical content knowledge of mathematics using a multi-agent large language model
text_snippet: Automated coding of content and pedagogical content knowledge of mathematics using a multi-agent large language model Abstract Despite the importance of content-specific knowledge for teaching, the task of measuring such knowledge, particularly pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), remains challenging. Scholars have been more successful in capturing the distinct nature of PCK when it has been assessed through open-ended response items, and such responses have been significantly linked to the quality of mathematics instruction and student learning. However, the use of open-ended items entails substantial resource and time demands, as it requires the training and ongoing calibration of human coders to ensure reliable coding of responses. Although scholars have explored technological approaches to automating coding, traditional automated methods have not achieved sufficient reliability for coding complex constructs, such as PCK. Advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities; however, it remains unclear whether existing LLMs are adequate or whether a purposefully designed LLM framework is required. In this study, we explored the potential of a multi-agent LLM, GradeOpt, which we developed to code mathematics content knowledge (CK) and PCK reliably, in comparison with commonly used au

title: Strategy-based motivation and learner-generated drawing: linking motivation and drawing processes in geometry modelling
text_snippet: Strategy-based motivation and learner-generated drawing: linking motivation and drawing processes in geometry modelling Abstract In this study, we examine the associations between strategy-based motivation (SBM) and how students construct and use drawings when solving geometry modelling problems. Sixty-six ninth- and tenth-grade students completed an SBM questionnaire assessing their expectancies of success, values, and effort intentions regarding the drawing strategy. They then solved six modelling problems while their eye movements were recorded using Tobii Glasses 3. Measures included effectiveness of drawing construction and use (derived from eye-tracking measures), drawing accuracy, and modelling performance (derived from scored drawings and solutions). Linear mixed models showed that expectancies of success and effort intentions were positively associated with the effectiveness of drawing construction and use, drawing accuracy, and modelling performance, although the variance explained by SBM was small. Findings support motivational theories by demonstrating that SBM is related to situated drawing processes as well as drawing and modelling outcomes.

title: Computational thinking and AI literacy integration in mathematics education: design principles for curricular and instructional innovations
text_snippet: Computational thinking and AI literacy integration in mathematics education: design principles for curricular and instructional innovations Abstract Integrating computational thinking (CT) and artificial intelligence (AI) to foster interdisciplinary learning has received much-needed attention worldwide in educational research, though less emphasis has been placed on simultaneously developing CT and AI learning outcomes in disciplinary (e.g., mathematics) classroom contexts. CT and AI are closely linked to mathematics, where knowledge of data practices, mathematical modelling, and generic skills such as problem-solving are highly emphasized. This paper reports on a design-based research study with four design cycles, aiming to generate empirically grounded design principles for curricular and instructional innovations in school mathematics contexts that simultaneously support CT and AI learning. Drawing upon the theoretical perspectives of CT as modelling and programming as white-boxing, and taking exemplary tasks developed from our design-based study, we detail four design principles: (1) Encourage tinkering with computational artefacts; (2) Leverage CT as modelling for authentic problem-solving; (3) Consider tool-based developmental trajectories; and (4) Exploit the white-box effect to foster mathematical and AI liter

title: Systematic survey of neurocognitive studies that examine connections between domain-general cognitive characteristics and mathematical processing
text_snippet: Systematic survey of neurocognitive studies that examine connections between domain-general cognitive characteristics and mathematical processing Abstract This systematic survey examines neurocognitive research on connections between mathematical processing and domain-general cognitive characteristics. From 1,798 initially identified papers, 83 studies met all inclusion criteria. We conducted a bibliometric analysis of temporal publication trends and leading journals, followed by a three-dimensional content analysis examining neurocognitive tools, mathematical characteristics, and domain-general cognitive characteristics across research designs, participant age groups, mathematical domains, and major findings. Analysis reveals predominant reliance on MRI (60%) and EEG (31%), with within-group mathematical task designs (70%) and between-group cognitive comparisons (60%) dominating approaches. Studies mainly focus on primary-school children (43%) and university students (39%), examining mostly arithmetic (63%) and number sense (33%). Critical gaps include underrepresentation of mid-to-high school students, limited investigation of mathematical abilities along the continuum, minimal use of advanced statistical methods, and infrequent separate neurocognitive assessment of cognitive processes. title: Student partnership in mathematics assessment: fostering student agency
text_snippet: Student partnership in mathematics assessment: fostering student agency Abstract Contemporary assessment research suggests that students should not be positioned as passive objects but as active agents. Nevertheless, student voices are rarely heard in assessment policy and practice. Even ‘student-centred’ practices are commonly built on compliance rather than ‘agency’, as they are often designed for students, not with them. In this study, we partner with students to co-design assessment and feedback in a Finnish secondary mathematics classroom. Our goal was to foster students’ agency and analyse whether this indeed happened. The co-designed assessment practices included, for example, a rubric, test items, and an e-portfolio. To capture the complexity of student agency, we present our findings in three parts, each emphasising different dimensions of agency. First, the assessment partnership process supported students’ agency over assessment artefacts as students took ownership over the materials they co-produced. Second, we explored agency with respect to social roles in assessment. While some students welcomed their redefined roles as active agents in assessment, others resisted. title: Complexity of geometrical problems as a function of field-(in)dependency and (a)symmetry of geometry diagrams: an ERP study
text_snippet: Complexity of geometrical problems as a function of field-(in)dependency and (a)symmetry of geometry diagrams: an ERP study Abstract Geometry is among the most challenging domains in middle school mathematics. While geometric problem solving depends on students’ spatial abilities and logical reasoning, problem complexity may also arise from task characteristics beyond students’ competencies. This study examines two diagram-related factors: field-(in)dependency (FID) and (a)symmetry (SYM). We hypothesize that geometry problems with identical conditions and goals become more complex when involving field-dependent (FD) rather than field-independent (FID) diagrams, and asymmetrical (ASYM) rather than symmetrical (SYM) diagrams, as reflected in behavioral measures and ERP amplitudes. Fifty-four Taiwanese high school students (Grades 10-11) solved geometry problems with different FID and SYM combinations while event-related potentials (ERP) were recorded to capture neurocognitive correlates of diagram complexity. The study findings supported our hypotheses: Students achieved higher accuracy with SYM or FID diagrams than with ASYM or FD diagrams. Response times were significantly longer for FD diagrams. title: The use of large language models to solve mathematical modeling problems: preservice mathematics teachers’ use practices, perceived affordances and challenges, and trustworthiness judgments of AI-generated outputs
text_snippet: The use of large language models to solve mathematical modeling problems: preservice mathematics teachers’ use practices, perceived affordances and challenges, and trustworthiness judgments of AI-generated outputs Abstract Mathematical modeling is a core component of mathematics education, enabling learners to connect mathematical ideas with real-world phenomena. Yet, it remains challenging for preservice teachers (PSTs), who must develop their own modeling competence while preparing to guide future students in reasoning about authentic situations. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising, though underexplored, potential to scaffold these complex learning processes by providing real-time explanations, supporting reasoning, and assisting with problem solving. This study examines how PSTs engage with LLMs while solving modeling problems, focusing on the perceived affordances, challenges, and trustworthiness of these tools, an essential aspect for developing critical and pedagogically responsible AI use in modeling. The study involved 150 PSTs enrolled in a master’s-level mathematics course at a German university who worked collaboratively on three authentic modeling tasks. Multiple data sources were analyzed, including worksheets documenting LLM-user interactions, open-ended survey responses, and semi-structured interviews. title: No one-size-fits-all: a study of prompt techniques and large language models to enhance AI’s mathematics educational quality
text_snippet: No one-size-fits-all: a study of prompt techniques and large language models to enhance AI’s mathematics educational quality Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly discussed as tools for supporting mathematical problem solving. However, existing research predominantly evaluates LLM performance in terms of correctness, while the mathematics educational quality of AI-generated worked-out solutions remains largely unexplored. This study investigates how the mathematics educational quality (a set of quality criteria relating to teaching and learning mathematics) of AI-generated problem solutions can be influenced by model choice and prompt engineering. Four LLMs (Gemini 1.5 Pro (Advanced), Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT-o3 mini, and DeepSeek-R1) were tested on six problem-solving tasks from the domains of number and algebra using four prompt techniques (Zero Shot, Chain of Thought, Persona, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation). In total, 2880 solutions were analyzed, combining human expert coding of content-related, process-related, and pedagogical-contextual quality with binary logistic regression. title: How relevant is mathematics for my field of study? Interindividual and context-dependent differences in students’ motivation and engagement with a mathematics prerequisites test across STEM fields
text_snippet: How relevant is mathematics for my field of study? Interindividual and context-dependent differences in students’ motivation and engagement with a mathematics prerequisites test across STEM fields Abstract Mathematics achievement difficulties contribute significantly to student attrition from postsecondary STEM programs. Many programs offer diagnostic tests embedded in preparatory or introductory mathematics courses to facilitate early identification and remediation of gaps in foundational knowledge. However, the utility of these tests depends on students’ test engagement and motivation—factors that can vary both among individuals and across STEM fields, depending on the perceived relevance of mathematics in each field. Guided by situated expectancy-value theory, this study examined interindividual and context-dependent differences in STEM students’ test-specific motivation, engagement, and performance on a mathematics prerequisites test ( $N = 2384$ N = 2384 ; 31 courses). Multilevel analyses revealed substantial between-course variation in test-specific achievement and motivation linked to course-level differences in prior mathematics achievement and motivation. text_snippet: Confronted with mathematics: the impact of pre-service elementary school teachers’ self-concept on emotional and physiological responses to mathematics exposure Abstract This study employed a situated approach to evaluate how female pre-service elementary school teachers’ mathematics self-concept impacts their emotional and physiological responses when confronted with mathematics tasks. We assessed participants’ ( $N = 70$ N = 70 , $M$ M age = 20.6 years) self-concept before inviting them into the laboratory, where they solved arithmetic pattern tasks. We recorded their psychophysiological arousal via skin conductance response (SCR), heart rate (HR), and heart rate variability (HRV), and assessed their situated emotional experience using self-report during task performance. We hypothesized linear associations between self-concept and subjective emotional valence (more pleasant with higher self-concept), and curvilinear associations between self-concept and psychophysiological arousal (higher arousal with both low and high self-concept). As predicted, higher self-concept was associated with elevated pleasant and reduced unpleasant emotional experience, even when controlling for task performance. title: Components of task values in a university mathematics course: trends, fluctuations, and relations to individual characteristics
text_snippet: Components of task values in a university mathematics course: trends, fluctuations, and relations to individual characteristics Abstract According to situated expectancy-value models, task values are important in mathematical learning processes. In university mathematics courses, some students devalue the mathematical content. To gain more insight into students’ task values during mathematics lectures, we analyzed the fluctuations of different task value components within and between lessons in a first-semester lecture in relation to individual characteristics. The participants in our study were 181 university mathematics students enrolled in a teacher education program. They reported their intrinsic value, attainment value, utility value for the study program, and utility value for professional life thrice in each lesson, for four lessons over one semester. At the beginning of the course, they reported individual characteristics. The results of variance decompositions and correlational analyses indicated that almost all task value components differ only marginally between lessons and time points, but substantially between students. title: Examining the role of drawing construction and use in mathematical modelling – an eye-tracking study
text_snippet: Examining the role of drawing construction and use in mathematical modelling – an eye-tracking study Abstract Learner-generated drawing has been identified as an approach to support mathematical modelling, especially in geometry problems. However, previous findings have been mixed, suggesting a drawing’s effectiveness depends on the quality of the drawing (i.e. drawing accuracy) and the quality of drawing processes. The aim of this research was to investigate students’ drawing processes while solving modelling problems and their relation to drawing accuracy and modelling performance. We employed a sequential mixed-method design using an eye-tracking methodology across two studies. In Study 1, to generate hypotheses about drawing processes and their relation to drawing accuracy and modelling performance, we qualitatively analysed gaze movements and stimulated recall interviews with six students solving a geometry modelling problem. In Study 2, we tested these hypotheses on a sample of 66 ninth- and tenth-grade students, who solved six geometry modelling problems while their gaze movements were recorded. title: Parental involvement, achievement and motivation: a longitudinal exploration of the interplay between parents’ practices and students’ mathematics achievement and motivation
text_snippet: Parental involvement, achievement and motivation: a longitudinal exploration of the interplay between parents’ practices and students’ mathematics achievement and motivation Abstract Research shows that parental involvement and specific parenting practices positively and significantly influence students’ motivation and academic achievement. Conversely, some findings indicate a different relationship in which parental assistance or support negatively correlate with academic performance and motivation. However, the cross-sectional design of many studies makes it difficult to determine whether parental support leads to lower academic achievement or if such a relationship arises because parents are more likely to offer support when their children encounter difficulties at school. This study clarifies the ambiguity by analysing three waves of student data (T1, T2, T3) and two waves of parent data (T1, T3). The data were collected from 420 fourth-grade students and their parents in Portugal across T1, with subsequent data collections for students in T2 (fifth-grade) and T3 (sixth-grade). In addition, we investigate the effects on academic performance and motivation of strategies promoting interest in mathematics and practices emphasising costs. title: Interlinking teachers’ beliefs and motivational practices: a cross-country examination of the relationship with students’ motivation in mathematics
text_snippet: Interlinking teachers’ beliefs and motivational practices: a cross-country examination of the relationship with students’ motivation in mathematics Abstract Building on previous research into teachers’ beliefs and practices in mathematics and their effects on students’ motivation, grounded in the situated-expectancy value framework, we combine person- and variable-centred approaches to examine changes in students’ motivation for mathematics as they transition to middle school. Using longitudinal data from 6656 students across six countries, we examined the slope of change in students’ motivation for mathematics and whether this trajectory is associated with specific constellations of mathematics teachers’ beliefs and practices. Four distinct teacher profiles emerged, with teachers belonging to all profiles in five out of six examined countries. Our findings indicate that each profile is uniquely associated with patterns that support or undermine different facets of students’ motivation for mathematics, suggesting a more complex relationship between teachers’ beliefs and practices and students’ motivation for mathematics.
